reason: Heat the rocky planetesimals to start exploring how stone and metal separate inside them.
expectation: Radioactive heating may melt or differentiate the rocky bodies, though the immediate result is uncertain.

alternatives.reason: Heating icy bodies could advance the water-in-rock goal, but I’ll follow the rocky branch first.

effect: The rocky body has melted, so gravity may now separate its materials.
reaction: The qualification that not all asteroids melt is useful.
reason: Apply gravity to the molten body to follow the rocky interior branch.
expectation: Denser metal may sink and separate from silicate rock.

alternatives.reason: I could start heating an icy body, but I want to finish the rocky branch first.

effect: Metal has separated into a core, so collisions may expose the differentiated materials.
reaction: It is satisfying to see gravity separate the molten body as expected.
reason: Use collisions to pursue the goal of exposing stone and metal from broken bodies.
expectation: A collision may break the differentiated body and expose rocky and metallic fragments.

alternatives.reason: Cooling the body also seems plausible, but collisions relate more directly to the goal.

effect: The collision exposed core metal; cooling the differentiated body may lead to the stone needed for the goal.
reaction: The link to iron meteorites makes the exposed core concrete.
reason: Cool the differentiated body to continue the rocky branch.
expectation: Its molten material may solidify, possibly producing rocky material that collisions can expose.

alternatives.reason: Heating icy planetesimals advances the other goal, but I’ll continue the rocky branch first.

effect: The asteroid now has a solid rocky exterior that a collision could expose.
reaction: Cooling before breaking the rock apart makes the sequence clear.
reason: Collide the cooled asteroid to pursue the exposed stone goal.
expectation: The collision may produce rocky fragments from its solid exterior.

alternatives.reason: Heating icy planetesimals would start the other goal, but I want to finish the rocky branch first.

effect: The rocky fragments complete the first goal; the remaining goal concerns water in altered rock.
reaction: The contrast between core and silicate fragments makes their different origins clear.
reason: Heat the icy planetesimals to begin the remaining goal; it is the only offered combination.
expectation: Radioactive heat may melt some ice and allow water to interact with rock.

effect: Internal heating produced liquid water that can now react with silicate rock.
reaction: The possibility of liquid water beneath a frozen exterior is interesting.
reason: Combine the water with silicate grains to pursue the remaining goal; this is the only offered combination.
expectation: Water may alter the silicate minerals and become incorporated into hydrated rock.

effect: Water reacted with silicates to form hydrated rock, completing the remaining goal and showing how hydrogen can travel inside rock.
reaction: The idea that rock can carry hydrogen after exposed ice is gone is a useful takeaway.

mostWorthwhile.text: Making water-bearing asteroid rock connected hidden liquid water to a plausible contribution to Earth’s volatile inventory.

leastWorthwhile.text: Cooling and then breaking the asteroid was clear but somewhat predictable, especially with compatible actions offered.

surprise.text: A frozen-looking body can contain liquid water, and hydrated minerals can retain hydrogen after exposed ice is gone.

arbitrary.text: Nothing felt purposeless; the cooling step’s role became clear when it solidified the rocky exterior.

continue.text: Yes, I would continue to see how these differentiated fragments and water-bearing rocks contribute to a growing Earth. The physical explanations made the progression engaging, though the offered combinations left little compatibility discovery.
